ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Transverse at the midpoint of the posterior arm. Injection sites follow the heads: long head at mid-arm and again 2 cm proximal, lateral head at mid-arm, medial head 1 cm distal to mid-arm.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Superficial and medial to the humeral cortex.
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Second only to the posterior deltoid among muscles injected for the extended shoulder. In biceps-triceps co-contraction, injecting triceps reduces resistance to passive elbow flexion.

clinical.function_biomechanics: At the shoulder the long head extends and adducts the humerus and supports the inferior joint (a taut long head resists inferior translation of the abducted arm — a “dynamic hammock” adjunct); it is the only biarticular head, so overhead elbow extension (throw, serve, press-out) loads it maximally; at the elbow all heads extend (anconeus assisting).
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: Shoulder level: none constant; distally the olecranon (subcutaneous) and subtendinous triceps bursae belong to the elbow. Adjacent structures — mutual influence: Quadrangular-space structures immediately lateral to its proximal tendon — hypertrophy/fibrous bands here are a described QSS mechanism; radial nerve/profunda at the triangular interval below; the infraglenoid origin transmits traction to the postero-inferior labrum (bennett-type posterior stress in throwers).

trigger_points.location: Five described triceps TrPs; shoulder-relevant is TrP1 in the long head, in the distal medial belly.
trigger_points.referred_pain: TrP1 refers upward to the posterior shoulder and down the posterior arm to the dorsal forearm, occasionally to the upper trapezius/neck base; (other heads: lateral epicondyle “tennis-elbow” pattern from TrP2, olecranon and medial-epicondyle/ulnar-digit patterns from the medial-head points).
trigger_points.source: Donnelly JM, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds). Travell, Simons & Simons’ Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual. 3rd ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2019. Muscle chapters as named in each section.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Into the posterior arm/shoulder strip: teres major/minor, subscapularis, latissimus, posterior deltoid, serratus posterior superior
C7 radicular pain runs the triceps line to the middle finger
quadrilateral-space pain sits at its proximal lateral border.
clinical.movement_restrictions_aggravators: Pain with overhead pressing/throwing follow-through and push-ups; end-range combined flexion+elbow-flexion stretch (hand-behind-head-and-down) reproduces.
clinical.notes: Isolated long-head weakness with intact wrist/finger extension is not a radial-nerve lesion — reconsider the axillary nerve/posterior cord.
clinical.caveat: Trigger-point locations and referral maps derive from the Travell–Simons clinical-observational tradition, now standardised by Delphi consensus criteria [32] and supported by prevalence and hyperalgesia studies in shoulder pain [30,31]; they are expert-level evidence, not trial-level, and inter-examiner reliability of TrP palpation is moderate. Facet, ACJ and subacromial referral patterns, by contrast, come from experimental provocation in volunteers/patients [33,34,37]. Textbook anatomy is cited at section level; where major texts disagree (segmental levels), the range is given and flagged. Figures and patterns older than 12 months are anatomical/physiological constants and are not considered stale.

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: The medial head is the primary extensor at every speed and load; the lateral and long heads are recruited with resistance. The three heads together have the largest cross-sectional area of any elbow muscle (about 15 cm² in Murray's series; 1.9 times the total flexor area by MRI), yet isometric extension torque averages only ~61% of flexion torque (Askew et al., 104 normal adults) because the extension moment arm (~2 cm) is roughly half that of the flexors. Extension torque, like flexion torque, peaks in mid-range flexion. Eccentric triceps work controls elbow flexion under load; concentric work drives push-off, crutch and wheelchair use, throwing and pressing. The long head also extends and adducts the shoulder and helps stabilise the humeral head in abduction. Retraction of the posterior capsule by the articularis cubiti fibres prevents capsular pinching in the olecranon fossa.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: Subtendinous olecranon bursa between the triceps tendon and the olecranon/posterior capsule; subcutaneous olecranon bursa over the olecranon (the usual site of olecranon bursitis); an inconstant intratendinous bursa. Adjacent structures and relations: Radial nerve and profunda brachii in the radial groove between lateral and medial heads; ulnar nerve on the medial head behind the medial intermuscular septum, then behind the medial epicondyle (snapping of the medial head over the epicondyle can accompany ulnar-nerve subluxation); posterior capsule and olecranon fossa fat pad deep to the distal fibres; anconeus laterally.

trigger_points.location: TrP1 long head, mid-arm on the medial side (the most common); TrP2 medial head, lateral distal fibres a few centimetres above the lateral epicondyle; TrP3 lateral head, lateral border of the arm; TrP4 medial head, deep and distal, just above the olecranon; TrP5 medial head, medial border, distal.
trigger_points.referred_pain: TrP1: up the posterior arm to the posterior shoulder with spill to the upper trapezius/neck, and down the dorsal forearm to the lateral epicondyle. TrP2: lateral epicondyle and radial forearm (a tennis-elbow mimic). TrP3: posterior arm, occasionally the dorsal forearm and 4th–5th fingers. TrP4: olecranon (mimics olecranon bursitis or insertional tendinopathy). TrP5: medial epicondyle, volar-ulnar forearm and 4th–5th fingers (a golfer's-elbow mimic). Anconeus TrPs refer to the lateral epicondyle.
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: Vague posterior arm ache, pain with forceful extension (pressing, push-ups, backhand), limited full flexion because of stretch pain; epicondylar tenderness attributed to tendinopathy; olecranon tenderness attributed to bursitis. Entrapment: TrP3 taut bands in the lateral head can compress the radial nerve in the spiral groove, adding dorsal-forearm and hand paraesthesia and extensor weakness. Associated TrPs: Latissimus dorsi, teres major, biceps and brachialis (antagonists), anconeus, hand extensors.
trigger_points.source: Travell & Simons, vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1999: ch. 32, Triceps brachii (and anconeus).

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: serratus posterior superior (deep scapular pain extending over the olecranon and ulnar forearm)
teres major and teres minor (posterior deltoid, over the long head)
coracobrachialis (posterior arm and dorsal forearm, skipping the elbow)
clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO the posterior arm / olecranon from elsewhere
clinical.notes: The lateral expansion is the anatomical basis of the anconeus–triceps sleeve used in Bryan–Morrey and related approaches; the ~0.88 tendon-to-olecranon width ratio guides repair. Triceps tendon ruptures affect the superficial (long/lateral) tendon more than the deep medial component. Snapping medial head and ulnar-nerve subluxation coexist.
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.

tests.name: Triceps rupture signs (palpable gap, weak or absent extension against gravity, modified Thompson squeeze)
tests.performance: Palpable gap, weak or absent extension against gravity, and the modified Thompson squeeze are the standard signs; Zwerus (2018) found no eligible accuracy studies for any triceps-rupture test. Partial tears typically preserve gravity extension, so resisted testing overhead is required.
tests.accuracy: Zwerus (2018) found no eligible accuracy studies for any triceps-rupture test.
tests.source: Zwerus EL, Somford MP, Maissan F, Heisen J, Eygendaal D, van den Bekerom MPJ. Physical examination of the elbow, what is the evidence? A systematic literature review. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(19):1253–1260.

clinical.tests_caveat: Values are taken from the cited primary studies. Most series are small and reference standards differ (surgery, arthroscopy, electrodiagnostics), so treat the numbers as indicative. The systematic review of Zwerus et al. (2018) found 24 described elbow tests, only 14 with any accuracy data, and concluded that no single test can rule an elbow diagnosis in or out on its own. Where no accuracy data exist, this is stated rather than estimated.
